  • Question 13. Explain the role of positive and negative controls. (3 Marks) [CO2,
  • • Definition and Need: Quality assurance/quality control (QA/QC) tools essential to
  • validate forensic testing protocols and ensure court-admissibility of DNA results — 1
  • mark
  • • Positive Control: A known standard DNA sample (e.g., 9947A, 007) run to verify that
  • extraction reagents, PCR master mix, primers, polymerase, and thermal cyclers
  • function correctly — (1 mark)
  • • Negative Control / Reagent Blank: Reaction without template DNA to detect
  • contamination, extraneous DNA introduction, or non-specific amplification across
  • reagents or laboratory handling — (1 mark)
  • Question 14. Explain the role of expert testimony in DNA evidence. (3 Marks)
  • [CO3, An]
  • • Objective Presentation: Explaining complex scientific methodology, collection
  • protocols, analytical techniques, and quality control procedures in clear,
  • understandable language to the court/jury — (1 mark)
  • • Statistical Interpretation: Presenting match probability, likelihood ratios, and
  • Combined Paternity Indices objectively without committing the prosecutor's fallacy or
  • defense fallacy — (1 mark)
  • • Ethical and Impartial Duty: Acting as an independent and impartial minister of justice,
  • evaluating limitations, artifact possibilities (stutter, drop-in/drop-out), and maintaining
  • scientific integrity — (1 mark)
  • Question 15. Discuss the importance of DNA discoveries in the development of
  • forensic science. (3 Marks) [CO1, K]
  • • Historical Paradigm Shift: Discovery of DNA structure (Watson and Crick) and forensic
  • profiling by Sir Alec Jeffreys (1984) revolutionized biological evidence from
  • exclusionary blood grouping to positive individualization — (1 mark)
  • • Exoneree Exoneration and Conviction Integrity: Provided an indisputable biological
  • gold standard for solving cold cases, identifying disaster victims, and post-conviction
  • exonerations of wrongfully convicted individuals — (1 mark)
  • • Establishment of Forensic Databases: Paved the way for standardized national DNA
  • databases (CODIS, NDNAD), automated STR typing, and enhanced speed and
  • reliability in criminal investigations — (1 mark)
  • Question 16. Discuss the usefulness of mitochondrial DNA in degraded
  • biological samples. (3 Marks) [CO2, U]
  • • High Copy Number per Cell: Hundreds to thousands of mitochondria per cell
  • compared to only two copies of nuclear DNA; significantly higher survival rate in aged,
  • burnt, or severely degraded remains — (1 mark)
  • • Suitability for Specific Matrices: Highly effective for telogen shed hairs lacking root
  • bulbs, desiccated bone fragments, ancient skeletal remains, and teeth — (1 mark)
  • • Maternal Lineage Tracing: Inherited maternally without recombination, allowing living
  • maternal relatives spanning multiple generations to serve as reference samples
  • (analyzing HV1 and HV2 regions) — (1 mark)
  • Question 17. Explain the importance of traceability in DNA analysis. (3 Marks)
  • [CO2, K]
  • • Chain of Custody: Complete, unbroken chronological documentation tracking
  • evidence collection, custody, transfer, analysis, storage, and court submission to
  • prevent tampering or substitution — (1 mark)
  • • Reagent and Equipment Calibration: Traceability of all chemical reagents, lot
  • numbers, pipettes, and thermal cyclers to certified reference standards under ISO/IEC
  • 17025 accreditation — (1 mark)
  • • Reproducibility and Auditability: Enables independent re-testing, validation of
  • standard operating procedures (SOPs), and defense scrutiny, ensuring courtroom
  • legal defensibility — (1 mark)

  • • Forensic Advantages of STRs: Small amplicon size (100–450 bp) ideal for degraded
  • samples; discrete allele designations based on integer repeat counts; low mutation
  • rates suitable for forensic tracking — (1.5 marks)
  • • Multiplex PCR and Capillary Electrophoresis: Simultaneous fluorescent amplification of
  • 15–24 loci in a single tube; high-resolution separation and detection via multi-capillary
  • electrophoresis with allelic ladders and internal size standards — (1.5 marks)
  • • Forensic Significance, CODIS and Discriminatory Power: Core loci utilized in national
  • databases (CODIS 20 core loci); extremely high discriminatory power where
  • cumulative random match probability exceeds 1 in a billion or trillion, providing
  • definitive individualization — (1.5 marks)
  • Question 23. Define DNA and explain its chemical composition and double-
  • helical structure. (6 Marks) [CO1, U]
  • • Definition and Cellular Organization: Deoxyribonucleic acid is the primary hereditary
  • biomolecule located in the nucleus (nuclear DNA) and mitochondria (mtDNA) that
  • encodes genetic instructions — (1.5 marks)
  • • Chemical Building Blocks (Nucleotides): Composed of repeating nucleotide units, each
  • comprising: (a) Deoxyribose sugar, (b) Phosphate group, and (c) Four nitrogenous
  • bases: Purines (Adenine , Guanine [G]) and Pyrimidines (Cytosine , Thymine [T])
  • — (1.5 marks)
  • • Watson-Crick Double Helical Model: Two antiparallel polynucleotide strands wound
  • around a central axis (5' to 3' and 3' to 5'); sugar-phosphate covalent backbone joined
  • by 3',5'-phosphodiester bonds; major and minor grooves — (1.5 marks)
  • • Complementary Base Pairing and Structural Stability: Specific complementary
  • hydrogen bonding: Adenine pairs with Thymine via two hydrogen bonds (A=T),
  • Guanine pairs with Cytosine via three hydrogen bonds (G≡C); hydrophobic base
  • stacking forces providing thermal and structural stability — (1.5 marks)
  • Question 24. Evaluate the suitability of hair as a source of DNA evidence and
  • discuss the factors affecting DNA recovery. (6 Marks) [CO2, E]
  • • Morphology and Growth Phases of Hair: Anagen (active growth, cellular follicular tag
  • rich in nucleated cells), Catagen (transition phase), and Telogen (shed/quiescent
  • phase, heavily keratinized with minimal/no nucleated pulp cells) — (1.5 marks)
  • • Nuclear vs. Mitochondrial DNA Suitability: Hairs with roots/follicular tags yield
  • abundant nuclear DNA suitable for autosomal STR profiling; shed telogen hairs lack
  • nuclear DNA and must be routed for mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) sequencing
  • (HV1/HV2) — (1.5 marks)
  • • Extraction and Lysis Protocols: Complete digestion of tough keratinized protein
  • matrices requires specialized chemical digestion: Proteinase K and strong reducing
  • agents (DTT - Dithiothreitol) to break disulfide bonds — (1.5 marks)
  • • Factors Affecting Recovery and Forensic Limitations: Environmental weathering (UV
  • sun exposure, microbial rot); cosmetic treatments (chemical dyes, bleaches, perming
  • agents act as PCR inhibitors or destroy DNA); root shearing/loss during forceful
  • extraction; lack of individualizing power if only mtDNA is recovered — (1.5 marks)
  • Part D – Essay Questions
  • Question 25. Define DNA variation and explain polymorphism, single nucleotide
  • polymorphism and their importance in genetic analysis. (15 Marks) [CO1, U]
  • • Definition of DNA Variation and Genetic Diversity: Concept of sequence variation
  • arising from mutations, insertions, deletions, and structural rearrangements across
  • the human genome; distinction between coding and non-coding variations — 3
  • marks
  • • Concept and Types of Genetic Polymorphism: Definition of polymorphism (existence
  • of two or more alleles in a population with frequency > 1%); Length polymorphisms
  • (VNTRs, minisatellites, STRs/microsatellites) vs. Sequence polymorphisms;
  • mechanisms generating variability (replication slippage, unequal crossing-over) — 4
  • marks
  • • Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs) - Characteristics and Detection: Definition of
  • SNPs (single base changes A/T/G/C); bi-allelic nature; low mutation rates (~10⁻⁸);
  • distribution across the genome (over 10 million SNPs); modern detection technologies
  • (microarrays, TaqMan assays, Next-Generation Sequencing / MPS) — (4 marks)
  • • Forensic, Medical, and Evolutionary Importance: Forensic individualization of severely
  • degraded samples using mini-SNPs; Biogeographical Ancestry (AIMs - Ancestry
  • Informative Markers); Phenotypic SNP profiling (HIrisPlex for eye/hair color);
  • pharmacogenomics and evolutionary phylogenetics — (4 marks)
  • Question 26. Evaluate the historical development of DNA profiling and critically
  • discuss its importance and applications in modern forensic science. (15 Marks)
  • [CO2, E]
  • • Historical Milestones and Genesis of DNA Profiling: Discovery of hypervariable
  • minisatellites and development of multi-locus probe (MLP) DNA fingerprinting by Sir
  • Alec Jeffreys (1984); Colin Pitchfork case (first criminal conviction and first
  • exoneration via DNA, 1986); transition to Single Locus Probes (SLP) and RFLP-
  • Southern Blotting (principles, limitations of high template requirement and radioactive
  • detection) — (3.5 marks)
  • • Technological Revolution - PCR, STRs, and Capillary Electrophoresis: Introduction of
  • Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) by Kary Mullis; evolution through HLA-DQA1 /
  • Polymarker dot-blots; development of automated fluorescent Short Tandem Repeat
  • (STR) typing; multiplex PCR systems and multi-capillary electrophoresis with laser-
  • induced fluorescence — (4 marks)
  • • Modern Applications in the Criminal Justice System: Violent crime investigation
  • (homicide, sexual assault); Mass Disaster Victim Identification (DVI - tsunami, 9/11,
  • aviation crashes); disputed paternity and kinship analysis; human trafficking, missing
  • persons tracing, and Cold Case resolution — (4 marks)
  • • Critical Evaluation, Advanced Frontiers, and Contemporary Challenges: Establishment
  • of national DNA databases (CODIS, NDNAD); emergence of Next-Generation
  • Sequencing (NGS/MPS), Rapid DNA systems, and Investigative Genetic Genealogy
  • (IGG); critical examination of challenges: low-template DNA artifacts, complex DNA
  • mixtures, contamination risks, secondary transfer, laboratory error rates,
  • ethical/privacy concerns, and genetic surveillance — (3.5 marks)
